The vignettes are on the package website,
<https://spriyansh.github.io/scMaSigPro/articles/>, and in R with
`browseVignettes("scMaSigPro")`; every function has a help page, such as
`?sc.squeeze`.

# Input

## What does scMaSigPro need from a trajectory?

One pseudotime value and one path label per cell, and the raw counts of the
cells. `as_scmp()` takes them as a `SingleCellExperiment` with two
`colData()` columns, `create_scmp()` as a count matrix and a data frame. See
the [Trajectory input](
    https://spriyansh.github.io/scMaSigPro/articles/trajectory-input.html)
vignette and the "Input contract" section of `?assign_paths`.

## How do I analyse a Monocle3 trajectory?

Take the principal graph, the nearest node of each cell, the root node and
the pseudotime from the `cell_data_set`, turn them into path labels with
`paths_from_graph()` and `assign_paths()`, and pass the counts and the cell
table to `create_scmp()`. The
[Trajectory input](
    https://spriyansh.github.io/scMaSigPro/articles/trajectory-input.html)
vignette has the code. Monocle3 itself is not a dependency, as it is not on
CRAN or Bioconductor.

## What about cells that belong to several paths?

Every cell gets one label. Cells on every path are the root, and cells on
some paths are a link, labelled with the names of those paths joined by
`_links_`; `assign_paths()` makes these labels from lineage weights, such as
those of slingshot. Then either analyse each segment as a path of its own,
or add the root and the links to the paths that share them with
`sc.restruct()`; the
[Shared root](https://spriyansh.github.io/scMaSigPro/articles/shared-root.html)
vignette compares the two.

## Raw or normalised counts?

Raw counts. The model is negative binomial, a distribution of counts, and
the offset of each bin accounts for its sequencing depth. For values that
are not counts, such as log-normalised or scaled data, use
`family = gaussian()` with `offset = FALSE` in `sc.p.vector()`.

## How many cells and bins are enough?

A polynomial of degree d has d + 1 coefficients per path, so each path needs
at least d + 1 bins, and a few more leave residual degrees of freedom for the
test. `plotBinTile()` shows the number of cells per bin; bins of very few
cells give noisy pseudo-bulk counts, which `prune_bins` removes and a lower
`drop_fac` avoids.

## The paths have different lengths. Does that matter?

Each path is binned along its own range of pseudotime, into a number of
bins that depends on its number of cells, and the model compares the paths
at the same binned pseudotime, the index of the bin. A path with more bins
extends beyond the others; `drop_trails = TRUE` in `sc.squeeze()` cuts the
longer paths to the binned pseudotime of the shortest, to compare only the
stretch they share.

# Settings

## Which bin rule should I use?

Sturges' rule, the default, is the rule of the analyses of the article;
`drop_fac` below 1 gives fewer, larger bins, useful for data with many
zeros, and `split_bins` and `prune_bins` even out the number of cells per
bin. The
[Model and tuning](
    https://spriyansh.github.io/scMaSigPro/articles/model-and-tuning.html)
vignette describes every rule and compares them, and `?estBinSize` gives
their formulas.

## Which test should I use for the full model, chi-squared or F?

`test = "chisq"`, the default and the test of maSigPro, treats the
estimated dispersion as known; with few bins it calls more genes
significant than its level. `test = "F"` accounts for the estimate and is
more conservative. The
[Model and tuning](
    https://spriyansh.github.io/scMaSigPro/articles/model-and-tuning.html)
vignette shows both.

## When should I turn the offset off?

When the data are not raw counts, such as normalised or scaled values, and
with any link other than the log link, which the offset needs. With raw
counts keep it: it corrects for the different numbers of cells, and so
depths, of the bins.

## How do I fit the genes in parallel?

Pass a BiocParallel backend to `sc.p.vector()` and `sc.t.fit()`, such as
`BPPARAM = BiocParallel::MulticoreParam(4)` on Linux and macOS or
`BPPARAM = BiocParallel::SnowParam(4)` on any system, Windows included. The
results do not depend on the backend.

## Are the results reproducible?

The workflow has no random step except the k-means clustering of
`sc.cluster.trend()`; call `set.seed()` before it for the same clusters.
Every setting a step used is kept in the object (`showParams()`).

# Results

## No gene passes. What now?

Check the bins first: too few bins, or bins of very few cells, leave the
test little to work with (`plotBinTile()`). Then the thresholds: `p_value`
of `sc.p.vector()` is, with the default correction, a false discovery rate,
and `rsq` of `sc.filter()` a threshold on the fit; `scmpResults()` reports
both values for every gene. On raw counts, turning the offset off can also
hide most genes, as the
[Model and tuning](
    https://spriyansh.github.io/scMaSigPro/articles/model-and-tuning.html)
vignette shows.

## Why do my results differ from those of version 0.0.4 or the 2024 article?

Version 0.6.0 changed how the bins are made and how the offset is computed,
honours the `link` argument and chooses the reference path in the same way
in every locale; each change is listed under "Changes affecting results" in
the [news](https://spriyansh.github.io/scMaSigPro/news/index.html). To
repeat an earlier analysis exactly, install the version that made it, for
example `BiocManager::install("BioBam/scMaSigPro@v0.0.4")`.

## I saved an object with an earlier version. Can I still use it?

Yes: run `updateObject()` on it after `readRDS()` or `load()`. The steps
stop with "update it with updateObject() first" until then. See
`help("updateObject,ScMaSigPro-method")` and the
[maSigPro and the ScMaSigPro class](
    https://spriyansh.github.io/scMaSigPro/articles/masigpro-and-class.html)
vignette.

## How do I get the results into my SingleCellExperiment?

`scmpToRowData(sce, scmp_ob)` writes the columns of `scmpResults()`, with
the prefix `scmp_`, into the `rowData()` of `sce`, matching the genes by
name.

## How long does an analysis take?

The fits run gene by gene, so the time grows with the number of genes and
with the number of bins; the number of cells matters only for the binning.
On the 100 genes and 16 bins of `splat.sim` the whole workflow takes well
under a second. A parallel backend fits several genes at a time.
